title: Chile's valleys
subtitle: Between the Andes and the Pacific
objectives: Explain the role of irrigation and the Andes

steps.title: A long, narrow country
steps.body: Chile is about 4,300 km long but rarely more than 180 km wide, between the Andes and the Pacific. Its isolation, protected by the Atacama desert in the north, the mountains, the ocean and Antarctic ice, has kept phylloxera out, so most vines grow on their own roots. The Central Valley holds most vineyards.

steps.title: Water from the Andes
steps.body: The Central Valley has a Mediterranean climate, with dry summers. Rivers fed by Andean snowmelt provide irrigation. Cold air flowing down from the mountains at night gives a wide day and night swing. Maipo, near Santiago, is Chile's historic Cabernet region; Colchagua and Cachapoal, in the Rapel Valley, make ripe reds.

steps.prompt: Why are most Chilean vines grown on their own roots?
steps.explanation: Natural barriers have kept phylloxera out, so grafting isn't needed.

steps.title: Carmenère
steps.body: Carmenère came from Bordeaux in the 19th century and was mixed up with Merlot. In 1994 it was identified, and it became Chile's signature grape. It needs a long, warm season; when ripe it gives dark fruit, spice and soft tannin; when unripe, a strong green pepper note.

steps.prompt: Match each Chilean valley to its focus.
steps.explanation: Chile's valleys differ by distance from the sea and the Andes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chile is long, narrow and free of phylloxera
Andean snowmelt irrigates the dry Central Valley
Carmenère, identified in 1994, is Chile's signature grape
